item.title: Macron vows legal action against perpetrators of violence in France protests
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
Around 550,000 people took part in protests across France on Saturday. According to local media reports, the demonstrations brought together farmers, climate activists, trade unions and students, who voiced demands concerning fuel prices, the cost of living, education and public services. PARIS, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday vowed legal action against those responsible for violence during protests across the country on Saturday. "Those who destroyed must pay. Those who looted must reimburse," Macron said in a televised address, pledging judicial proceedings over offenses committed during the violence. He voiced support for law enforcement officers, elected officials and shopkeepers affected by the violence, adding that Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu would chair a crisis unit Monday to mobilize "the fastest possible assistance" and support those affected. He called on the government to draw all the lessons from Saturday's violence, particularly regarding intelligence gathering and anticipation, to ensure such incidents "cannot happen again." Meanwhile, Macron said he understood the "deep anxiety" expressed by young people in recent weeks at high schools and universities, adding that over the coming week, the government would work with students, teachers, trade unions, employers' organizations and officials to develop responses to young people's concerns. Macron said the protests also reflected public concerns over the cost of living and fuel prices. He said the government was doing its utmost to address the key issue of residents' purchasing power. Around 550,000 people took part in protests across France on Saturday. According to local media reports, the demonstrations brought together farmers, climate activists, trade unions and students, who voiced demands concerning fuel prices, the cost of living, education and public services. A total of 2,397 people were arrested during the protests, which were marred by violence, according to figures released by the French Interior Ministry on Sunday. A total of 997 police officers and gendarmes were injured, seven of them seriously. Since September, France has witnessed multiple rounds of mass student protests demanding better educational conditions.

item.title: LatAm journalists explore drivers of China's NEV industry
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18
by Xinhua writers He Yixuan, Xi Yue, Zhao Yanchao CHANGZHOU, China, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Cameras clicking and smartphones raised, a group of Latin American journalists moved through the production workshops of a Chinese new energy vehicle (NEV) maker in Changzhou, east China's Jiangsu Province, capturing robots at work and vehicles taking shape on the assembly line. For some, the scene offered a glimpse into the technology behind Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) they had already seen on the streets back home. Thousands of kilometers away, Chinese-made EVs are becoming part of everyday life in Latin America, while charging facilities and power transmission projects are opening up new avenues for green cooperation. During the 2026 Belt and Road Journalists Forum, dozens of journalists from Latin American countries visited Changzhou, known as China's "capital of new energy," to explore the industrial strengths behind China's green development and discover opportunities for cooperation with Latin America. FROM FACTORY FLOORS TO EVERYDAY MOBILITY For Rody Olivera, president of the Uruguayan Press Association, the visit was more than a tour of a manufacturing facility. Having purchased a Chinese NEV in May, he was eager to see how it was made. Inside the welding workshop at Li Auto's manufacturing base in Changzhou, he said the visit had confirmed that he had "made the right decision." "The factory is impressive in terms of its size and productivity. Electric vehicles offer many advantages, as they provide a quieter driving experience, numerous driver-assistance features and greater comfort," Olivera said. In his view, China's progress in the sector stems from both policy support and industrial capabilities. "China is a pioneer in this technology," he said, attributing the country's achievements to its innovation capabilities and the development of a complete industrial chain. At the exhibition hall of Segway-Ninebot, a renowned electric two-wheeler maker, Angel Sanchez, president of the Federation of Journalists of Peru, recognized the company's electric scooters, saying they could offer a convenient transportation option for young people and office workers in Peru. "They have many advantages, including quick responsiveness, flexible center-of-gravity control and a portable design," Sanchez said, adding that China's development of new energy and other emerging technologies ultimately aims to improve people's lives. Such products offer a glimpse into the broader industrial ecosystem that has taken shape in Changzhou. Its industrial chain spans five areas: energy generation, storage, transmission, consumption and distribution networks. In 2025, the scale of the city's new energy industry exceeded 1 trillion yuan (about 150 billion U.S. dollars). CONNECTING INDUSTRIAL STRENGTHS WITH LOCAL NEEDS The city's industrial strengths extend from NEVs and key components to charging infrastructure and power transmission equipment, creating opportunities for cooperation across different stages of the energy transition. At the exhibition area of charging infrastructure operator Star Charge, Virgilio Arias, president of Mexico's Front Page Club, stopped in front of a photograph showing an electric-bus charging station in Mexico City. "I've just learned that this Chinese company has provided charging facilities for three Bus Rapid Transit lines in Mexico City and Monterrey, supporting the operation of more than 150 electric buses," Arias said. The example highlighted how Chinese technologies are being applied to local transportation systems in Latin America. As Mexico and other countries in the region accelerate their energy transitions, cooperation in charging infrastructure and electric mobility could help address practical needs while advancing shared sustainable development goals, Arias said. Green cooperation also extends beyond transportation to the infrastructure needed to transmit clean energy over long distances. For Samira de Castro, president of the National Federation of Journalists of Brazil, a visit to NR Electric brought an unexpected connection to a project she had covered years earlier. In 2012, she wrote a report on Brazil's Belo Monte hydropower project. During her visit in Changzhou, she learned that the company's technology had been used in the project's second-phase ultra-high-voltage transmission system. Now operational, the transmission project helps deliver hydropower from northern Brazil to distant consumption centers, including areas serving Rio de Janeiro. Castro said the advanced technology had made a significant contribution to Brazil's electricity supply and changed the lives of local residents. TURNING SHARED GOALS INTO GREEN COOPERATION "There is an ecosystem of companies here that are collaborating to advance clean energy. Renewable energy is the future, and it is happening right here, right now," said Geraldo Cantarino, a member of the Brazilian Press Association, during his first visit to China. For Latin American countries with diverse energy resources and growing demand for cleaner development, cooperation with China could create further opportunities in equipment manufacturing, infrastructure construction and the application of new energy technologies. For the journalists visiting Changzhou, the trip offered a closer look at the industrial capabilities underpinning China's new energy development and their potential relevance to Latin America. From EVs and smart mobility products to charging networks and power transmission systems, the examples they encountered demonstrated how green cooperation can take shape across an interconnected industrial chain. As the visit drew to a close, the journalists took away more than photographs of production lines, electric scooters and power transmission equipment. They had also gained a firsthand understanding of how technologies developed in a Chinese industrial hub could connect with the green development ambitions of countries across Latin America. For Castro, the next step was to share these observations with a wider audience. "As a journalist, I hope to tell more people the stories of China-Latin America cooperation in the new energy sector, so that the world can see China's commitment to high-quality development, openness and cooperation," she said.■

item.title: Chinese, international buyers gather at ceramic expo in China's "porcelain capital"
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18
NANCHANG, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- The 2026 China Jingdezhen International Ceramic Expo opened on Sunday in Jingdezhen, a city in east China's Jiangxi Province famed as the "porcelain capital," attracting more than 1,000 professional buyers from home and abroad. The five-day event showcases several facets of the ceramic industry, including the entire industrial chain, its domestic and international markets and its application of digital technology, all within an exhibition space of 140,000 square meters. It has brought together exhibitors from over 19 countries, including Spain, Germany and Japan. Themed zones feature creative design, smart ceramic manufacturing, international brands, and ceramic-producing cities. The 2026 standards for the "Jingdezhen Made" regional brand and the city's digital culture and tourism platform were unveiled at the opening ceremony. On July 25, the Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, filling a long-standing gap in the list for porcelain heritage and becoming China's 61st World Heritage site. The heritage sites represent the handicraft porcelain industry system that developed in Jingdezhen from the 10th to the 19th century. Today, Jingdezhen's ceramic industry chain employs over 100,000 people, and the comprehensive division-of-labor system that once underpinned its historic success continues to thrive. First launched in 2004, the expo has not only continued to broaden its international reach but also gradually built a comprehensive platform integrating exhibition and trade, cultural exchange, and investment cooperation. With a population of over 1.6 million, Jingdezhen recorded a net population inflow of 136,000 over the past decade. Among those who have started long-term businesses in the city, more than half come from outside Jiangxi Province, with a notable number from overseas. ■

item.title: Liangzhu forum opens, highlights heritage conservation, int'l cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18
Lina Mendoni, Minister of Culture of Greece, addresses the opening ceremony of the fourth Liangzhu Forum in Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, Oct. 18, 2026. The fourth Liangzhu Forum opened Sunday in Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, to discuss challenges in cultural heritage conservation and paths to deepen international cooperation. The year 2026 marks the 90th anniversary of the discovery of the Liangzhu ruins. Themed "Bridging the Past and the Future: Safeguarding Cultural Heritage for Our Times," the forum brings together officials, archaeologists and scholars from around the world. (Xinhua/Xu Yu) HANGZHOU, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- The fourth Liangzhu Forum opened Sunday in Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, to discuss challenges in cultural heritage conservation and paths to deepen international cooperation. The year 2026 marks the 90th anniversary of the discovery of the Liangzhu ruins. Themed "Bridging the Past and the Future: Safeguarding Cultural Heritage for Our Times," the forum brings together officials, archaeologists and scholars from around the world. Experts and scholars will discuss topics ranging from early civilizations to archaeological research on ancient cities, with new research findings and advances also set to be unveiled, Zhang Ling, an official with China's National Cultural Heritage Administration, said at an earlier briefing. Participants will address challenges including the loss of cultural heritage, advances in technologies for protecting and utilizing cultural relics, and sustainable tourism, Zhang added. Lina Mendoni, Minister of Culture of Greece, said in a speech at the opening ceremony that people must move beyond traditional approaches and adopt adaptive, preventive and holistic management to safeguard cultural heritage. "UNESCO believes that sustainable tourism can help safeguard cultural heritage by raising awareness of the importance of heritage for future generations, improving cultural understanding and strengthening local livelihoods," said Nayef Al-Fayez, UNESCO Assistant Director-General for Culture, in his video speech. The forum brings together four international organizations: UNESCO, based in Paris; the International Centre for the Study of the Preservation and Restoration of Cultural Property, headquartered in Rome; the Alliance for Cultural Heritage in Asia, based in Beijing; and the International Alliance for the Protection of Heritage, headquartered in Geneva. The gathering marks a step for the forum to turn into a broader venue for multilateral dialogue on cultural heritage, said Wen Dayan, another official with the National Cultural Heritage Administration. This year's event includes an opening ceremony and main forum, five sub-forums and five companion events, including an international artists' creative tour exhibition, a Liangzhu cultural and creative market, a design exhibition and international dialogues. Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2019, the Archaeological Ruins of Liangzhu City offer important evidence of an early regional state that flourished more than 5,000 years ago. The inaugural forum was held in Hangzhou in 2023. The fourth edition runs through Tuesday and is co-hosted by China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism, the National Cultural Heritage Administration and the Zhejiang provincial government. ■ Delegates from the National Cultural Heritage Administration of China and the International Centre for the Study of the Preservation and Restoration of Cultural Property shake hands after signing a memorandum of understanding on cooperation during the opening ceremony of the fourth Liangzhu Forum in Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, Oct. 18, 2026. item.title: China railway passenger trips hit record high in first three quarters
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18
BEIJING, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- China's railway network handled 3.71 billion passenger trips in the first three quarters of 2026, up 4.8 percent year on year, the highest for the period, according to the China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway). During the period, the railway network operated an average of 11,511 passenger trains daily, up 5.3 percent from a year earlier. Railway departments have actively responded to demand for sightseeing, wellness tours and red-themed study tours, according to China Railway. In the first nine months, a total of 2,860 tourist trains were operated across the country, up 25.5 percent year on year. The railway network also operated 947 special trains for concertgoers and sports fans during the period, effectively boosting the catering, hotel and cultural tourism sectors. Cross-border rail travel also continued to grow. The China-Laos Railway carried 265,000 cross-border trips, up 37.8 percent, while the Guangzhou-Shenzhen-Hong Kong high-speed railway handled over 25.8 million cross-border trips, up 11.8 percent, China Railway said. China Railway also adapted to the inbound travel boom created by the country's visa-free transit policy. The railway network carried over 19 million foreign passenger trips in the first three quarters, up 33.4 percent year on year, the company said. Behind the steady growth in passenger traffic is China's increasingly dense high-speed rail network. By the end of 2025, the country's total operating railway mileage had reached 165,000 km, which included more than 50,000 km of high-speed rail. On Sept. 28, China opened four high-speed rail sections, connecting Xiongan in north China's Hebei Province with Shangqiu in Henan Province in central China, Xi'an with Ankang in Shaanxi Province in northwest China, Yichang with Xingshan in central China's Hubei Province, and Harbin with Yichun in Heilongjiang Province in the country's northeast. China's high-speed rail network is projected to hit 70,000 km by 2035, featuring eight north-south vertical lines and eight east-west horizontal lines. Once complete, the network will connect major cities, city clusters and key economic zones across the country. ■

item.title: Chinese premier says ready to advance high-quality Belt and Road cooperation with Tajikistan
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18
Chinese Premier Li Qiang holds talks with Tajik Prime Minister Kokhir Rasulzoda in Dushanbe, Tajikistan, Oct. 18, 2026. Following the talks, the two sides witnessed the signing of multiple documents covering infrastructure development, education, anti-corruption and standardized cooperation. (Xinhua/Ding Lin) DUSHANBE, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang said on Sunday that China stands ready to work with Tajikistan to advance high-quality Belt and Road cooperation. He made the remarks in talks with Tajik Prime Minister Kokhir Rasulzoda during his official visit, saying China is willing to deeply align its development strategies with Tajikistan, deepen cooperation in trade and investment, green minerals, connectivity, clean energy, artificial intelligence and other areas, so as to better achieve mutual benefit and win-win results. China will import more high-quality goods from Tajikistan, encourage Chinese enterprises to invest and start businesses in Tajikistan, and hopes that Tajikistan will continue to provide a favorable business environment for enterprises, Li added. Both sides should expand exchanges and cooperation in areas such as culture, education, health, sports and local-level fields to enhance the sense of gain of the people of both countries, said Li, noting that at the same time, the two countries should continue to deepen law enforcement and security cooperation to foster a stable and secure environment for personnel exchanges between the two sides. Noting that the international situation continues to undergo complex changes, Li said that as important members of the Global South, China and Tajikistan should unite and coordinate more closely, safeguard the common interests of both countries and defend international fairness and justice. He said the two sides should further strengthen communication and coordination within multilateral frameworks including the United Nations, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, the China-Central Asia mechanism and the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, and work to build a more just and equitable global governance system. People of China and Tajikistan have always shared friendly sentiments toward each other, Li said, noting that in recent years under the strategic guidance of President Xi Jinping and President Emomali Rahmon, China-Tajikistan relations have maintained a high level of development, with cooperation across various fields deepening and yielding tangible results. Next year marks the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations between China and Tajikistan, Li said, adding that China stands ready to work with Tajikistan to deepen strategic mutual trust, firmly support each other, take all-round cooperation to new heights, deliver more tangible outcomes and better benefit people of both countries. For his part, Rasulzoda said that under the strategic guidance of the two heads of state, Tajikistan-China relations are currently at their best level in history. In May this year, Tajik President Emomali Rahmon paid a successful visit to China, and relations between the two countries have entered a new stage of development, Rasulzoda said. China is the most important trade and investment partner of Tajikistan, Rasulzoda said, expressing appreciation for China's long-standing and strong support for Tajikistan's economic development. He said Tajikistan is committed to advancing all-round cooperation with China and stands ready to further leverage such platforms as the China-Tajikistan intergovernmental committee on economic and trade cooperation, promote high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, and deepen mutually beneficial cooperation in trade, investment, agriculture, transport and logistics, energy and minerals, and connectivity. Rasulzoda also called for expanding cooperation in emerging fields such as the green economy, digital economy and artificial intelligence, enhancing people-to-people exchanges, and strengthening communication and coordination within multilateral frameworks, including the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and the China-Central Asia mechanism, to promote further progress in Tajikistan-China relations. Following the talks, the two sides witnessed the signing of multiple documents covering infrastructure development, education, anti-corruption and standardized cooperation. On Sunday afternoon, Li also laid a wreath at the monument of Ismoil Somoni. ■ Chinese Premier Li Qiang holds talks with Tajik Prime Minister Kokhir Rasulzoda in Dushanbe, Tajikistan, Oct. 18, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Ling)

item.title: Xinhua Headlines: Inside China's "unlikely" AI computing hub
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18
* In less than two years, Inner Mongolia's computing capacity has nearly quadrupled, reaching 363,000 petaflops by August 2026, as large-scale data centers have sprung up across the region. * However, the region is not content to remain a mere "landlord of data centers." It is striving to move up the value chain, reinventing itself not only as a hub for green computing but also for token trading and AI applications. * With the influx comes new challenges. Computing facilities require enormous amounts of electricity to run and water to keep server racks from overheating. Inner Mongolia, a frontrunner in China's green energy transition, is charting a course of green computing. HOHHOT, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- A four-hour drive northwest of Beijing takes one across the Great Wall and into the grasslands of Inner Mongolia, seemingly a world away from China's booming coastal towns. Yet here, in a city once known as China's "potato capital," data centers are rising from the grasslands, towering cranes fill the skyline, and some of the country's biggest tech companies are moving in. The city is Ulanqab, in the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, which has emerged as a new frontier in the global race for computing power. Ulanqab is a poster child for this rise. In less than two years, Inner Mongolia's computing capacity has nearly quadrupled, reaching 363,000 petaflops by August 2026, as large-scale data centers have sprung up across the region. A combination of factors helped fuel this transformation. Its climate allows natural cooling of AI server racks for nearly ten months a year. The windswept steppes offer a massive volume of wind and solar power, driving rates down to as low as around 0.35 yuan (about 5.2 U.S. cents) per kWh. Moreover, its proximity to Beijing ensures an ultra-low latency of under 5 milliseconds, facilitating seamless model training and real-time inference. However, the region is not content to remain a mere "landlord of data centers." It is striving to move up the value chain, reinventing itself not only as a hub for green computing but also for token trading and AI applications. RISING ABOVE GRASSLAND At the Ulanqab Chahar High Tech Development Zone, the epicenter of the city's newfound buzz, an "Apple Boulevard" runs alongside an "Alibaba Boulevard" and a "Huawei Boulevard" -- named after three of the major companies that have set up a presence here. Other tech giants, including ByteDance, Kuaishou and VNET Group, have also moved in. Vehicles from across China line the roads, and workers speak in accents from every corner of the country. Around lunchtime, food stalls spring up around the construction sites, selling boxed meals, fruit and drinks. "Within the high-tech zone alone, 22 computing-power projects are currently under construction, involving nearly 30,000 construction workers," said Liu Junping, deputy director of the administrative committee of the development zone. "When I came here to scout the site in 2022, it was still pretty desolate, and sandstorms would sometimes sweep through," recalled Zhou Yiguang, an executive with the VNET Group's Ulanqab base. The group has planned a computing cluster covering 1,100 mu (about 73 hectares) of land in Ulanqab, and the first phase has been in operation since October 2024. In fact, it is not just Ulanqab. Inner Mongolia has emerged as a hub for computing power, with its regional capital Hohhot as another high ground. As of the first half of 2026, roughly 20 of China's 30 leading private computing companies had established a presence in the region, with combined investment exceeding 200 billion yuan (around 29.75 billion U.S. dollars). In addition, nine of the country's top 10 computing service providers had also set up operations there. GREEN COMPUTING With the influx comes new challenges. Computing facilities require enormous amounts of electricity to run and water to keep server racks from overheating. Inner Mongolia, a frontrunner in China's green energy transition, is charting a course of green computing. In 2025, the computing industry in Ulanqab alone consumed 4.3 billion kWh of electricity. That figure is estimated to reach 9 billion kWh in 2026 and will continue to surge as more computing centers are expected to start operating over the next two to three years. Globally, tech giants are moving beyond simply "buying power" to "competing for power" and even "generating their own power." China, however, has leveraged its world-leading power grid, renewable energy and energy storage industries to pioneer the integration of computing power and electricity supply, known as "computing-electricity coordination." In the Ulanqab Chahar High Tech Development Zone, a zero-carbon industrial park is taking shape. The park will be managed as a unified power distribution unit, with wind and solar infrastructure developed collectively by the government, then distributed to individual computing centers across the park. Chen Zhigang, deputy director of the Ulanqab municipal development and reform commission, said that the park's surrounding areas have about 10 gigawatts of wind and solar development capacity available. Once tapped, these resources could generate more than 30 billion kWh of electricity annually, enough to cover future increases in demand. After the zero-carbon industrial park is completed, more than 80 percent of the park's electricity will come directly from renewable energy. In the Horinger New Area in Hohhot, computing centers in operation source 85 percent of their power consumption from green energy. Water poses another potential constraint. However, widespread adoption of water-conserving cooling equipment, such as waterless fluorine-pump air conditioning systems and closed cooling towers, helped ease the high demand for cooling water. Moreover, take VNET Group's cloud computing center in Ulanqab for example: here, outdoor cold air is directly used for cooling for nearly 10 months of the year, with spray systems activated only during the hottest summer days. "All the water used for cooling at the computing center is reclaimed water. It does not affect local natural water resources or groundwater," said Li Yi, technical director of VNET Group's Ulanqab base. According to the Ulanqab water resources bureau, under the regional regulations, data centers are prohibited from using groundwater as cooling water. In 2025, big data companies across the city consumed 1.54 million cubic meters of water, accounting for only 0.33 percent of the city's total water consumption. Meanwhile, the city produces about 72 million tonnes of reclaimed water annually. TOKEN HUB Building computing capacity is one thing, yet turning it into a high-value AI economy is another. "If we rely solely on cheap electricity and low land costs, we risk becoming little more than 'landlords of server rooms,'" Liu Huansuo, deputy director of the Ulanqab big data administration, warned. The concern is well-founded. The high-value segments of the computing economy -- chips, algorithms and models -- remain largely beyond Inner Mongolia's reach. According to economic data from Ulanqab, the city's computing-power industry generated 6.835 billion yuan in revenue in 2025, with 368 million yuan in tax revenue. A computing center is estimated to create about 100 jobs per 100 mu (about 6.7 hectares) of land. Yet these returns remain modest relative to the massive upfront investment in infrastructure and the enormous computing capacity that is being developed. To address the challenge, Inner Mongolia strives to move up the value chain -- evolving from a "server-room landlord" to a "token capital," and cultivating its own ecosystem of AI applications. On May 30, Inner Mongolia's Token Trading Platform, billed as the country's first green-computing full-stack AI platform, went into operation in the Horinger New Area, positioning Hohhot to become a major token-trading hub in northern China. The goal is to turn raw computing power into a tradable commodity that can be measured, priced and ultimately converted into higher-value AI services, said Guo Juying, deputy director of the Horinger New Area Administrative Committee. She described the transition as a shift from "selling electricity" to "selling tokens," as every AI conversation or model inference can ultimately be measured in terms of tokens generated and consumed. Ulanqab has its own plan. At the end of 2025, the city released a three-year action plan for building a "Token Capital" for 2026-2028, envisioning a new economic chain spanning the production, trading and application of tokens. The application ecosystem is also expanding. Hohhot has developed nearly 100 application scenarios in sectors such as dairy, new energy and biomedicine. A facial recognition database for cattle is already widely used on smart pastures. For a region that has built its computing infrastructure at remarkable speed, the next challenge may be harder. But overcoming it will open up a whole new horizon across China's economic landscape. ■ (Video reporter:Zhang Sheng; Video editors: Hong Ling, Zhang Mocheng and Hong Yan)
